title: I can’t code. Shipped a full boxing RPG to iOS anyway
author: ChampChase_
selftext:
started in january with zero gamedev experience and i have not hand written a single line of code. Its been live on testflight since may - story campaign with 50+ fights, training and economy systems, arena seasons, original soundtrack, \~1000 voiced lines. A pixel art boxing rpg called ChampChase

my first attempts failed exactly how you'd expect. one long chat session, codebase slowly drifts until nothing compiles and neither me nor the Al could tell which change broke it. what i figured out way too late is that throughput was never the problem — knowing what was actually TRUE after each change was the problem

so the setup that ended up working: multiple claude code sessions in parallel, each one owns its own set of files (fight engine, campaign, ui, audio, saves...) with a dumb lock file system so they physically cant touch each others stuff. While I sit in a 7th window assigning work and keeping the big picture

The whole thing cost \~800€ in tooling

Happy to answer any questions about the process or anything related

replies.author: MessageSelfdestructs
replies.body:
I come from 15 years of professional gamedesign (level design and 3D artist), and I've encountered the same challenges in gamedesign companies: getting it out the door is always the hardest part.

As such, I was a bit more known with the pitfalls of designing (or rather, delivering) a game, and it made my journey I started 2 years ago slightly easier.  
I've created 2 games with AI since then (coding/concept art/pixel art/sound), with moderate sales results (84k and 41k last time I checked), and am currently working on my third game (and updating my second game where needed).

However, my personal advice would be if your current game is going to get you some profit, is to keep using AI, but to not disclose it in the future: currently there's too much of a sentiment of people who really look at AI-usage as a bad thing in design, and this might negatively affect your sales.

I personally think it's nobody's business what tools I use, however I'm quite the perfectionist, so I spent quite a lot of time on polishing my games before release.  
One aspect that I pointed out in your game is the graphics - these are most of the times the first thing that people will notice it's created by AI.  
I of course had a bit of a head start, since I've been designing (digital) art since I was a little kid, and I was able to convert my 3D skills into 2D/pixel art skills, and as such was able to generate most of my art with the help of AI, but then spent lots of time polishing that art to make it look handmade (which to some extent, is true).

But yeah, the TL;DR is pretty much: try to keep your AI-usage quiet.  
Do not see it as if you're abusing your customers by not disclosing it.

The most important thing for a customer/player is that the game plays well, and is fun.

Nothing else.

So as such, where possible, try to make your game as fun as possible, and as polished as possible, and try to cover up the main tells of a game being created by AI.

I've been able to not disclose it, and with my two games released, I've only had one accusation at one point from someone who said it was AI - I was able to doctor some images to "prove" them wrong, even though that wasn't really necesary to do from my side either: I could have ignored them, but I also saw it as a challenge. :-)

But yeah, keep up the good work, dude. If this is your first project, you're going to move mountains. Over the next few years you'll be come better with all aspects of gamedesign, and how to use/improve AI.

Good luck!

TL;DR: if possible, try to not disclose you've used AI for your game, as it can only lead to lost sales, which is ridiculous if your game is fun to play.
